title: Casper and the Machine
premise: Coral Lockridge, a nonbinary navigator who fled the war by taking a dead-end post tending a navigation beacon at the system's edge, shares their station with the 'sleepers' — memory backups of the beacon's original crew, including a partial copy of Coral's dead mother, stored in the hold and legally nobody. When gravity across the entire system stutters for nine seconds, Coral discovers the beacon isn't a beacon at all: it is the receiver half of a weapon-arming handshake, and the nine-second flicker was the sender waking up. Hunted by both warring fleets who each want to control the handshake, Coral must carry the sleepers — including their mother's backup, who may remember why she really died — to the sender station and choose whether to broadcast an armistice key that will end the war or trigger mutual disarmament that could be read as surrender. In the end, Coral lets their mother's backup finish the transmission and then finally let her go, choosing the living crew they've gathered over the ghosts in the hold.
about_author: Jonah Voss is the pen name of a former merchant-marine radio operator who spent six years on long-haul freighters before turning to fiction. They write quiet, character-driven science fiction about people who keep machines running after everyone else has stopped caring.

chapters.title: Nine Seconds of Falling
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. During a routine calibration, gravity across the whole system flickers for exactly nine seconds; Coral's tea rises, dust hangs, and the beacon logs an inbound handshake it shouldn't recognize. The emotional beat is dread disguised as routine — Coral has built a life out of being forgotten, and something just remembered them.

chapters.title: The Hold Full of Sleepers
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, with flashback texture. We meet the backups: forty-one dormant memory cores of the beacon's original crew, including one labeled L. LOCKRIDGE. Coral talks to them like coworkers because the station is otherwise silent. Emotional beat: loneliness so old it has become ritual.

chapters.title: Ping from the Dark
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A ship answers the handshake ping — not a fleet vessel but a scavver tug captained by Dez Okonkwo, a charming ex-naval engineer fleeing debt. Dez claims the flicker fried their drive and begs dock rights. Coral, against every instinct, says yes. Beat: the first crack in Coral's isolation.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Actually Is
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. While patching their drive, Dez finds the beacon's secondary lattice — a receiver array for an arming handshake, decades old, still warm. They don't tell Coral everything. Beat: guilt and curiosity wrestling; Dez needs salvage money more than they need a clear conscience.

chapters.title: Mother, Partial File
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A power surge wakes the L. LOCKRIDGE core for ninety seconds. Coral's mother's backup doesn't recognize the adult Coral — she thinks Coral is eight years old and asks about homework. Beat: grief reopened; Coral shuts the core down with shaking hands and lies to themselves about why.

chapters.title: The Fleet Arrives Early
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. A Republic corvette drops out of fold near the station, demanding inspection. Dez hides the array schematics; Coral stalls the boarding officer with bureaucratic perfection. Beat: fear sharpening into resolve — invisibility is officially over.

chapters.title: Both Sides Want the Key
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Intercepted traffic reveals the Concordat also knows about the handshake; whoever completes it controls the armistice key buried in the sender station's code. Coral realizes the 'beacon maintenance' job was a cover someone gave them deliberately. Beat: paranoia curdling into purpose.

chapters.title: Dez's Ledger
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Coral catches Dez transmitting station schematics to a broker. Confrontation in the airlock corridor; Dez confesses the debt, the family on Ceres Station, the arithmetic of betrayal. Coral doesn't space them. Beat: anger giving way to a hard bargain — help me fly this thing, or I turn you in.

chapters.title: Waking the Crew
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. To fly the beacon's ancient tug frame, Coral spins up three sleeper cores as advisory intelligences: engineer Amara Sen, pilot Yusuf Kane, and, last and hardest, their mother. Beat: found family assembling itself from the dead, each voice carrying its own grief.

chapters.title: Departure Window
chapters.summary: Yusuf's core POV (rendered as log entries). The ragtag crew threads the Republic blockade using a trick only a dead pilot would know. Beat: exhilaration — Coral feels competent and accompanied for the first time in years.

chapters.title: The Mother Problem
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Aboard, the mother-core begins remembering forward — reconstructing memories past her death date, including fragments of why she was aboard the beacon when it was destroyed. She asks Coral to stop calling her 'the file.' Beat: tenderness and terror entangled.

chapters.title: Concordat Interception
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. The Concordat cruiser Vantage hails them with a genuine offer: safe passage and debt forgiveness for the array codes. Dez, tempted, looks at Coral and lies to the cruiser instead. Beat: loyalty chosen, not assumed — Dez burns their way home.

chapters.title: Amara's Confession
chapters.summary: Amara Sen's core POV. She reveals the original crew didn't die in an accident: they scuttled the beacon to bury the handshake, and Coral's mother cast the deciding vote. Beat: inheritance reframed — Coral's exile was designed by the person they miss most.

chapters.title: Gravity Remembers
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A second nine-second flicker hits mid-transit, worse — planets visibly shudder, and the sender station is clearly waking without them. Time pressure becomes existential. Beat: panic transmuted into velocity.

chapters.title: The Republic's Kind Face
chapters.summary: Yusuf's core POV. Captain Ilse Marr of the Republic offers Coral everything: rank restoration, amnesty, a real crew — if Coral hands over the key for 'controlled decommissioning.' Coral hears their own loneliness being weaponized. Beat: temptation met with clarity.

chapters.title: Sabotage in the Hold
chapters.summary: Dez's POV. Someone — a stowaway Republic tech planted during the earlier inspection — tries to fry the sleeper cores. Dez takes a plasma burn saving the mother-core. Beat: Dez fully crosses from mercenary to family; Coral stops keeping score.

chapters.title: What My Mother Chose
chapters.summary: Mother-core POV. Her reconstructed final memory completes: she voted to scuttle the beacon because the key could also start the war, and she stayed behind to make sure no one ever finished the handshake. She tells Coral the choice was always theirs to remake. Beat: blessing, at last.

chapters.title: Running the Gauntlet
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV rotation. Both fleets converge on the sender station; the crew flies a suicide-thin corridor between bombardment lines, Amara riding the engines, Yusuf flying dead reckoning through debris. Beat: the found family functioning as one organism under fire.

chapters.title: The Sender Room
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Inside the station, the handshake console waits, and both fleet boarding parties arrive seconds apart with weapons drawn. Coral stands between them, holding the key, and makes the case neither side wants to hear: the key ends the war only if both sides believe the other will press it too. Beat: the climax of nerve — one small person refusing to move.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Mother-core POV, handing off to Coral. Together they transmit the armistice key on open channels — unencrypted, undeniable, disarming everyone equally. Fleets freeze; the nine-second silence returns, then breaks into stunned chatter. Beat: catharsis; the machine finally does what it was built for.

chapters.title: Letting Go of the Hold
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. With the war ended, the sleeper cores face mandatory archival erasure. Coral sits with each one — Amara, Yusuf, and last their mother, who thanks them for the homework answer, thirty years late. Beat: grief completed instead of deferred; inheritance passed on willingly.

chapters.title: A Crew of the Living
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, epilogue. Coral, Dez, and the rescued Republic tech sign aboard a refitted beacon-station turned relay post — a lighthouse again, honestly labeled this time. The last line mirrors the opening: gravity holds steady, and Coral's tea stays in the cup. Beat: quiet hope; staying visible, together.
